rationale: Start with a broad, moderately fast gradient to locate all eight peaks and identify critical pairs while limiting the risk of non-elution. The middle temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Raise temperature while holding the gradient fixed to test selectivity changes in the four-peak cluster and late doublet. All peaks currently elute well before 10 minutes, leaving time to flatten the gradient later if needed.

Flatten the gradient substantially at the better-performing temperature to test whether the close pairs separate with greater retention. The previous elution window suggests this should keep all eight peaks observable and may keep the last peak near 10 minutes.

Lower temperature by one step to shift selectivity around the sole remaining critical pair while preserving the successful shallow gradient. This tests whether temperature can complete the separation without extending the gradient.

Use a shallower gradient to improve the remaining close pair at 55 C, while raising the starting organic fraction to offset the added retention time. The aim is full resolution with the last peak at or below 10 minutes.

At 60 C the earlier cluster was better resolved; a shallower gradient may now separate the remaining late pair. Raising the starting organic fraction to 0.20 should help keep the last peak below 10 minutes.

Test the low-temperature selectivity regime using the original gradient for a direct comparison. The high-temperature methods leave different critical pairs unresolved, so a larger temperature change may reveal a better separation pattern.
Flatten the gradient at 25 C to improve the two moderately under-resolved pairs. The last peak at 6.34 minutes leaves substantial room to gain resolution without a time penalty.

The middle pair appears to approach an elution-order crossover as the gradient becomes shallower; flatten further to seek separation beyond that crossover. Raise the starting organic fraction to help keep the last peak within 10 minutes.

Slightly flatten the best gradient by lowering phi1 one step, aiming to lift the sole critical pair from R = 1.40 above 1.5. The 0.75-minute margin before the time penalty should accommodate this small change.

The maximum CRF is secured at injection 10; now test a higher starting organic fraction at the same gradient slope to shorten the fully resolved separation. Check whether the modest resolution margins survive the earlier elution.

Flatten the gradient at the faster 0.20 starting fraction to recover resolution of the sole critical pair. This should trade some of injection 11's time savings for full resolution while remaining faster than injection 10.

Raise the starting organic fraction to accelerate elution, while flattening the gradient to protect the critical middle pair. This tests whether full resolution can be retained in less than injection 12's 9.18 minutes.

Raise temperature one step from the fastest fully resolved method to test whether elution can be accelerated without losing resolution. Keep the gradient fixed to isolate temperature-dependent changes in the critical pairs.

Test whether a further temperature step moves the late doublet beyond its apparent selectivity crossover and restores separation in a shorter run. Injection 13 remains the fastest fully resolved fallback while we check for new critical pairs.

Apply the 30 C temperature step to injection 12's fully resolved gradient. Its stronger late-pair separation at 25 C may provide enough margin to avoid the late doublet seen in injection 14 while shortening retention.

With maximum CRF already secured, test a substantially faster gradient on the steep side of the middle-pair crossover. A temperature of 30 C may improve the late pair that limited the original fast 25 C separation.

Lower temperature at the fast gradient to test whether the middle cluster opens up, as it did in the initial temperature comparison. This isolates temperature selectivity while checking whether the late pair remains sufficiently resolved.

Return to the fully resolved 25 C regime and test a higher starting fraction with a substantially shallower gradient to protect the middle pair. This probes whether further window narrowing can shorten the separation while retaining the maximum score.

Slightly steepen injection 14's gradient to test whether the late doublet gains enough selectivity to reach R ≥ 1.5 in a shorter run. Monitor the middle pairs closely, since their resolution margins were small.

Use a slope between injections 11 and 12, closer to the fully resolved injection 12, to approach the resolution boundary from the safer side. This may retain R ≥ 1.5 for every pair while slightly improving on the fastest fully resolved separation.

Test a slightly steeper slope than injection 13 at the same starting fraction and temperature, seeking a faster fully resolved separation. Injection 21 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score method if the critical middle pair falls below R = 1.5.

Slightly steepen injection 21's gradient to probe the fastest fully resolved boundary, while shortening the programmed gradient. Its critical pair was only just above R = 1.5, so retain injection 21 as the confirmed maximum-score fallback.

Test whether a higher starting fraction at 30 C opens the early cluster while this intermediate slope separates the late doublet. The maximum score is already secured, so this is a final targeted search for a faster fully resolved method.

Use the final injection to seek a larger resolution margin than injection 12 by slightly flattening its gradient, with the last peak expected to remain below 10 minutes. Injection 21 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method, and the campaign has already achieved the maximum CRF of 1.000.
